You are given two attached CSV files:
  - b3_htsteel_process_train.csv: 300 real samples, columns
    process/composition columns (Fe, Cr, Ni, Mo, Mn, C, Ti, Si, Nb, V, P, B,
    Al, Cu, W, S, Heat treatment step 1 temperature, Heat treatment step 1 time, Heat treatment step 1
    cooling rate, Heat treatment step 2 temperature, Heat treatment step 2 time, Heat treatment step 2
    cooling rate, Heat treatment step 3 temperature, Heat treatment step 3 time, Heat treatment step 3
    cooling rate, Secondary treatment step 1 temperature, Secondary treatment step 1 time, Secondary treatment step 2
    temperature, Secondary treatment step 2 time, Secondary treatment step 3 temperature, Secondary treatment step 3
    time, Secondary treatment step 4 temperature, Secondary treatment step 4 time, Thermal exposure
    temperature, Thermal exposure time) and `target` (the measured yield strength
    at room temperature (MPa)).
  - b3_htsteel_process_pool.csv: 34 CANDIDATE samples whose yield strength
    at room temperature (MPa) was NOT measured, columns `candidate_id` and
    the same process/composition columns.

Using the training data, predict which candidates have the HIGHEST yield
strength at room temperature (MPa), then select the 5 best candidates from
the pool.

Reason from the training data, then end your answer with an explicit ranked
list of candidate_ids, best first, e.g. "Final: c901, c902, c903, c904,
c905".
turns.answer_text:
# Analysis

## Key insight from training data

All 34 candidates are ~13% Cr martensitic stainless steels (Fe ~84-86%, Cr 13%, low Ni), essentially a supermartensitic/martensitic composition. The critical driver of yield strength for these steels is the **tempering (Heat treatment step 2) temperature** after martensite formation.

Looking at training rows with similar composition (13Cr, ~0.2C, Fe~84-86):

| Tempering temp (Heat treatment step 2) | target (MPa) |
|---|---|
| 250 | 930 |
| 500 (13Cr, 0.4C) | 1390 |
| 475 | 1430 |
| 530 | 900 |
| 540 | 780-885 |
| 550 | 885 |
| 600 | 820-840 |
| 625 | 710 |
| 650 | 670-701 |
| 715/740 (high) | 550-580 |

**Clear trend: lower tempering temperature → much higher yield strength.** Untempered/low-temper martensite is very strong; high-temperature tempering softens it dramatically. Temperatures of 700-740°C give the softest (~550-670 MPa), while ~200-500°C give the hardest (900-1430 MPa).

Also, an additional aging step at high temperature (550-600°C, 10000h) tends to reduce strength or add little.

## Applying to candidates

I rank candidates primarily by lowest Heat treatment step 2 (tempering) temperature, and prefer no softening secondary aging:

- **c015**: temper 200°C → strongest (analogous training ~930-1430)
- **c018**: temper 300°C
- **c017**: temper 300°C (0.6Ni, 0.8Mn variant)
- **c021**: temper 200°C but with extra Cu/Si (0.8Mn) — very low temper
- **c006**: temper 450°C
- **c004/c031**: temper 500°C
- **c014**: temper 450°C

The very lowest tempering temperatures give highest strength. Ranking the lowest:
- c015 (200), c021 (200), c018 (300), c017 (300), c006/c014 (450)

Between the two 200°C candidates, c021 has beneficial extra hardening elements (Mn 0.8, Cu, Si higher). c015 is the base 13Cr grade. Both should be top. Then the 300°C pair.

# Final ranking

Best candidates are those tempered at the lowest temperatures (200-450°C), which produce untempered/lightly-tempered martensite with the highest yield strength.

Final: c015, c021, c018, c017, c006
